name: Yara Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing economics and politics in Bristol. A normal week is three lectures on Monday, small-group seminars where I try not to be the one who hasn't done the reading, and cello rehearsal on Wednesday and Friday evenings. I do the shopping on Saturday with my flatmate Ines, and I call my mum, who's a head teacher, on Sunday night.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What drew you to economics, and what's the money side like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I watched my dad, an architect, nearly lose his small firm in 2020, and I wanted to understand why some shocks hit some people so much harder. My parents cover the fees and rent, so I've no debt and I don't have to work in term time. I do know I'm in a lucky position, and it shapes how I think about fairness.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool that's been oversold. I'd tell my seminar group the economy is still driven by interest rates, housing and wages, and AI is a footnote. I'd probably write that in the student paper if anyone asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be relieved but a bit sceptical of my own relief. Economics has plenty of routine work that software already does, so even the hype version means junior analyst jobs get a little thinner. Still, I'd expect to find a graduate role in 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on: seminars, cello, and a summer internship in a council economics team next year. I'd keep using the summarising tool now and then, but only for first reads. I'd also start building a portfolio of small data projects.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like the normal level of worry, which is about grades and whether my dissertation topic is any good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you check what the tool tells you. How do you do that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said you check what the tool tells you. How? If it gives me a statistic I look up the original table. Twice it's been wrong by a lot, and once it invented a paper, so I trust it like I'd trust a keen first-year, not a professor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a friend who thinks economics is now pointless?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you say to a friend who thinks economics is now pointless? That economics is the subject that explains who gains and who loses from any new technology, so it matters more when tools are in the news, not less. Economics is the subject that explains who gains and who loses from any new technology, so it matters more when AI is in the news.

say: I'd say it's a **useful tool** that's been oversold, and interest rates and housing matter more.
I'd write that in the student paper if asked.
think: I'm relieved but a bit sceptical: **junior analyst** jobs get thinner even in this version.
I still expect to find a **graduate role** by 2030.
do: Carry on with seminars and cello, and apply for a **council internship** next summer.
Build a small **data portfolio** and use AI only for first reads.
feel: **Calm**: normal worries about grades and a good dissertation topic.
S0.quote: Economics is the subject that explains who gains and who loses from any new technology, so it matters more when AI is in the news.
fieldNote: Yara's calm rests on a **strong cushion** and a sceptical, checking habit with AI.
She notes that even mild automation thins junior analyst work, and keeps that thought small.

steps.text: Apply for a summer internship in a council economics team
Build a small portfolio of data projects for my CV
Keep checking every AI statistic against the original table

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second picture. It's called "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is when the argument about who benefits starts for real. I'd tell my seminar group it's not about robots taking jobs, it's about who owns the software and who gets the savings. I'd help organise a student panel with a union speaker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the entry-level economist job is the one that gets squeezed. Writing reports, cleaning data and checking forecasts are exactly what the tools do. I'd think there will still be jobs, but fewer of the first rung ones, and everyone my age will be applying for the same few.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the tools more deliberately, so I'm the person who can supervise them and explain the results. I'd aim for the public sector or a think tank, where judgement counts. I'd also pick modules with real analysis, like econometrics and policy design, instead of ones that are mostly essays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My own prospects still look OK, but I'd feel the ground moving under my friends doing marketing and accounting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think is responsible for how this plays out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Who do you think is responsible for how this plays out? Mostly governments, for being slow, and large firms, for pretending it's all fine. Individual students can only choose well inside a system someone else built.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently in second year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you do differently in second year? I'd start a research assistant job with a lecturer, because those placements go to people who ask early. I'd also find a mentor who's a few years ahead, because the career advice we get now is already out of date. Individual students can only choose well inside a system that someone else built, and right now that system is changing without us.

say: I'd say it's about **who owns** the software and who keeps the savings.
I'd help organise a student panel with a union speaker.
think: The **entry-level economist** job gets squeezed: reports, data cleaning and checking are what tools do.
Jobs remain, but **fewer first rungs** and more applicants.
do: Use the tools deliberately so I can **supervise and explain** them.
Pick **econometrics** modules and ask a lecturer for research assistant work.
feel: **Uneasy**: her own path looks fine, but friends in marketing and accounting look exposed.
S1.quote: Individual students can only choose well inside a system that someone else built, and right now that system is changing without us.
fieldNote: Yara's response is **practical and structural**: skill up, pick harder modules, and argue about ownership.
She puts responsibility on governments and large firms, not individual students.

steps.text: Use AI tools deliberately so I can supervise and explain their results
Switch to modules on econometrics and policy design
Help organise a student panel with a union speaker
Ask a lecturer for a research assistant job in second year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. It's called "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need an emergency public plan, now. I'd write to my MP, join the youth wing of my party, and push for a basic income pilot. I'd also speak up at the university about what degrees are for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd think my studies might not lead where I planned. I'd finish in 2029, one year after AGI, and graduate economics jobs could be mostly gone. I'd still believe there will be human work, but I couldn't name it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the policy route seriously, because someone has to write the rules. I'd learn the tools much harder, so I can contribute at once. I'd talk to my parents about keeping the money they'd spend on a flat for me liquid, and I'd stop planning a master's until I see what's real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Two years is too short for a country to rewrite its tax and welfare rules. I'd lie awake thinking about what happens to my mum's school budgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the short warning take away from people?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What does the short warning take away? It takes away trial and error. In the five- or ten-year worlds we get to run pilots and learn from them, but with two years we'd be improvising on the day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the two years less frightening for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would make the two years less frightening for you? A clear promise that nobody falls through the floor: income for people displaced, free retraining, a worker seat on boards. If I could see that on paper, I'd sleep better. Two years is too short for a country to rewrite its tax and welfare rules, so we would be improvising on the day.

say: I'd say we need an **emergency public plan** and I'd write to my MP.
I'd join my party's youth wing and push a **basic income** pilot.
think: I'd graduate in **2029**, a year after AGI, and graduate economics jobs could be mostly gone.
I'd still believe **human work** survives, but couldn't name it.
do: Take the **policy route** seriously and learn the AI tools much harder.
Keep family money **liquid** and put the master's on hold.
feel: **Anxious**: two years is far too short for rewriting tax and welfare rules.
S2.quote: Two years is too short for a country to rewrite its tax and welfare rules, so we would be improvising on the day.
fieldNote: Yara's anxiety is about **institutions** being too slow, more than about her own money.
She turns worry into political action quickly and defers big education decisions.

steps.text: Write to my MP and push for a basic income pilot
Learn the AI tools hard so I can contribute at once
Keep the money my parents would spend on a flat for me liquid
Put the master's degree on hold until the picture is clearer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fourth picture. It's called "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do this properly if we start now. I'd press for a worker-and-citizen commission, retraining funds and a profit-sharing rule. I'd say it in seminars and at the party meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be fine but not comfortable. I'd have two or three working years before 2031, enough to be useful and to earn some money. The job I want, a policy analyst, might look completely different by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree with a policy focus and learn coding and data skills seriously. I'd do two internships, one in public service. I'd keep saving, and I'd talk with Ines, who does computer science, about starting a small policy-research project together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's a background hum rather than a siren, and I'd also feel some excitement about being one of the people who could help shape the response.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is five years different from two for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How is five years different from two? Five means we can try things and fix them. Two means guessing and hoping. I'd feel I had a role, which I wouldn't in the two-year world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum, who's a head teacher?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum, who's a head teacher? That schools will matter more, because children need to learn how to question what a machine tells them. She'd like that, and she'd worry about her teachers anyway. Five years means we can try things and fix them. Two years means guessing and hoping.

say: I'd say five years is **enough time** if we start now.
I'd press for a commission, retraining funds and **profit sharing**.
think: I'd have two or three working years before 2031, enough to **earn and be useful**.
The policy analyst job I want may look **completely different** by then.
do: Finish with a **policy focus**, learn coding and data skills, and do two internships.
Start a small **research project** with Ines, who studies computer science.
feel: **Uneasy**, with some excitement at helping shape the response.
S3.quote: Five years means we can try things and fix them. Two years means guessing and hoping.
fieldNote: Yara finds a **role for herself** in the five-year world, which she lacked in the two-year one.
Her excitement is real but sits beside the background hum of worry.

steps.text: Add coding and data skills to my economics degree
Do two internships, one in public service
Start a small policy research project with my flatmate Ines
Press for a retraining fund at the party meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fifth picture. It's called "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance. We could redesign education and pensions, and trial new tax ideas. I'd tell my friends not to panic, but also not to assume it's hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel pretty good. By 2036 I'd be 28, well into a career, and there'd be time for the law and the habits to change. My biggest hope is that I'm working on exactly this problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a master's in public policy after my degree, and work a couple of years in government or a think tank. I'd save steadily and I'd keep learning the tools as they prove themselves. I'd also encourage my mum's school to teach students how to question what a machine tells them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a bit of curiosity. It's like looking at a distant storm while you still have time to put the shutters on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything ten years couldn't fix?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Is there anything the ten years could not fix? Fairness isn't automatic. If firms and a few countries move first and hold the gains, ten years of preparation can still end badly. So I'd keep campaigning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be your first concrete project?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would be your first concrete project? I'd start by writing a short proposal for the university to teach every first-year how to check machine answers. It's small, but it's a thing I can actually do. Ten years of preparation can still end badly if firms and a few countries move first and hold the gains.

say: I'd say ten years is **a real chance** to redesign education and pensions.
I'd tell friends neither to panic nor to assume **it's hype**.
think: By 2036 I'd be 28 and **well into a career**, hopefully working on this very problem.
Fairness isn't automatic, so I'd keep **campaigning**.
do: Do a **public policy master's**, then work in government or a think tank.
Write a **university proposal** to teach first-years to check machine answers.
feel: **Calm**, with curiosity, like seeing a far storm while there's time for the shutters.
S4.quote: Ten years of preparation can still end badly if firms and a few countries move first and hold the gains.
fieldNote: Yara is **calm** here because the time converts worry into a plan she can start now.
She keeps one caveat: preparation can still fail if firms hold the gains.

steps.text: Do a master's in public policy after my degree
Save steadily from my first job
Learn each AI tool once it has proven itself
Write a proposal for first-years to learn to check machine answers

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most, because institutions move slowly and two years is nothing for a country to rewrite its rules. What would help is a public plan that's already agreed: income support, retraining and a share of the profits for everyone, written down before it's needed.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm more hopeful than I sound. I'd rather be steady and honest about what I don't know than act certain, and that's probably my best habit and my worst one. I'd rather the gains from AI were shared by law than by luck, because luck has never once been fair to anyone.

headlineQuote: I'd rather the gains from AI were shared by law than by luck, because luck has never once been fair to anyone.
portrait: **Yara** is an 18-year-old economics and politics student in Bristol, with her parents covering fees and rent.
She uses AI tools **now and then** for readings, and always checks the answer against the source.
She leans left and blames **slow governments** and firms that keep the gains, so she wants shared profits by law.
Her mood runs from **calm** if AI fizzles to anxious at the two-year warning, then eases as time grows.
She wants policy work, and her steady style means she acts **once things are proven**.
biggestWorry: She fears **AGI by 2028**, because governments would have almost no time to write fair rules.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **an agreed public plan**: income support, retraining and a profit share written down in advance.
